extracted.intended_audience: lay Christian readers seeking Puritan moral and devotional instruction (17th-century parishioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and signs for judging whether a person's repentance/conversion is genuine or spurious, and signs of a godly vs. impenitent death, presented in a didactic Puritan narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sight and sense of sin required for repentance
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance is not produced without a sight and sence of sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly asserts that genuine repentance requires a person to have sight and sense of their sins (examples: the three thousand in Acts 2, Paul, the jailor, David after Nathan). Without this interior awareness one cannot be sorry for sin or turn from it. Mr. Badman lacked this at death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of true repentance
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance is a being sorry for, and a turning from transgression to God by Jesus Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author corrects the misconception that repentance is mere confession; instead it is sorrow plus a turning away from sin toward God through Christ. This definition is used as the touchstone for judging whether apparent penitence is genuine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sick‑bed repentance is often spurious
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance on a deathbed is seldom good; it commonly seeks only to be saved from Hell or to have life prolonged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs of spurious sick‑bed repentance include cries born of fear of punishment, conditional promises 'if God spare me I'll amend', and short-lived vows that vanish after recovery. The author likens such repentance to 'the howling of a dog' and warns it often passes away like a mist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confession alone insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Many think Repentance stands in Confession of sin only, but they are mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that confession without turning and lasting change does not equal saving repentance; mere verbal admissions do not suffice. Examples: those who confessed or begged prayers but returned to former ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not every sight/sense of sin produces saving repentance
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sight and sense of sin cannot produce repentance unto salvation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even persons (Cain, Pharaoh, Saul, Judas) who had great sight/sense of sin nevertheless lacked repentance unto life. Thus presence of conviction alone is not decisive — one must examine resulting fruit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire to remain in security indicates lack of repentance
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who desires to remain in security and resists discourse about their sin shows they do not truly desire repentance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Badman could not endure that any man should talk to him of his ill‑spent life; he preferred carnal company and resisted godly admonition. Avoidance of convicting conversation is presented as evidence of impenitence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Welcoming worldly company vs. receiving godly counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: A sick person's hospitality toward old worldly companions and coldness toward good men is a sign of hypocrisy/impenitence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts hearty reception of carnal companions with chilly, evasive behavior toward godly visitors. Preference for worldly conversation in sickness is anti‑evidence of genuine conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of life, word (Scripture), and death as proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance is judged by comparing a person's life, the Word, and their death together — true repentance manifests consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists those that knew Mr. Badman compared his life, the Scripture's teaching, and his dying actions to determine absence of repentance. Durable, life‑long conformity to Christ's ways and scripture at death vindicates repentance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of a godly death
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of a good death includes expressions of comfort and assurance, longing for heaven, signs of joy, music/peace at departure, and exhortations to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: the wife who 'died bravely' with many 'brave Expressions' and longing for the Bridegroom, and the godly old man whose attendant heard 'Musick' as his soul departed. Such signs are presented as consolations and as proof of saving grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symptoms of impenitent death
rubrics_metrics.description: Dying without repentance is indicated by lack of sense of sin at death, return to former ways after recovery, and death in a state of security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Badman is described as secure and without sense of sin in his final sickness; he returned to his debaucheries after earlier fits. The text warns that such an end brings misery and a 'name [that] shall rot.'

rubrics_metrics.name: True repentance includes desire for Christ's righteousness and sanctifying Spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine converts desire Christ's righteousness to clothe them and the Spirit to sanctify them, not merely escape punishment or gain worldly benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes Mr. Badman did not desire Christ for his righteousness or the Spirit for sanctification; his desires were temporal (avoid Hell, prolong life). The presence of longing for Christ's saving righteousness is a positive marker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruit (changed actions and affections) over mere words
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincere repentance is shown by real change in conduct and affections (e.g., sustained love, godly living), not merely by flattering words made in crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative shows many who made vows when sick but did not amend when well; genuine conversion produces lasting changes such as godly counsel to children, choosing godly company, and continued devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public reputation and memory as consequences of life/death
rubrics_metrics.description: The memory and reputation left behind reflect the moral quality of a person's life and death: 'The memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked shall rot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses social aftermath (neighbors' judgments, 'name rotted above ground') as a posthumous test or consequence of the reality of one's moral state and repentance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral tests when visited by good men
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific observable behaviors toward virtuous visitors serve as tests of sincerity (e.g., feigning faintness, evasive replies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator begins to list a 'Character of his carriage to good men' (first: 'When they were come, he would seem to fail in his spirits at the sight of them'), suggesting that particular actions and mannerisms when confronted with godly counsel are evidence to assess.
